title: What must Australian charities do so board members understand their duties under ACNC Governance Standard 5?
description: The seven duties in ACNC Governance Standard 5, the reasonable steps a charity takes so board members understand them, and the evidence to keep for the ACNC.
shortAnswer: Under ACNC Governance Standard 5, set out in section 45.25 of the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Regulations 2022, a registered charity must take reasonable steps to ensure its Responsible Persons, such as board or committee members and trustees, are subject to and comply with seven duties. The Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC) expects charities to bring the duties to their attention, provide regular information or training, and act when duties are not met.
keyTakeaways: Section 45.25(2) lists seven duties: reasonable care and diligence, good faith in the charity's best interests and purposes, not misusing position, not misusing information, disclosing material conflicts of interest, managing financial affairs responsibly, and not allowing the charity to operate while insolvent.
The obligation sits on the charity: it must take reasonable steps to ensure Responsible Persons are subject to, and comply with, the duties.
The ACNC's suggested steps include letters of appointment or a board charter that set out the duties, regular information or training, and asking Responsible Persons to undertake training.
Four statutory protections in sections 45.105 to 45.120, including a business judgment rule, treat the charity as having taken all reasonable steps when a Responsible Person meets them.
Compliance with the Governance Standards is a condition of registration; serious breaches can lead to warnings, directions or revocation. Basic Religious Charities are exempt.
jurisdiction: Australia (Commonwealth): Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Act 2012 and Regulations 2022
appliesTo: Charities registered with the ACNC, other than Basic Religious Charities
Responsible Persons: board and committee members, directors and trustees
Directors of a corporate trustee of a charitable trust
Company secretaries, CEOs and governance officers who support the board

blocks.text: Governance Standard 5 requires a registered charity to take reasonable steps to ensure its Responsible Persons are subject to, and comply with, seven duties. The standard is section 45.25 of the [Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission Regulations 2022](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2022L01301/latest/text), where the regulation uses the term "responsible entities"; the ACNC's guidance calls them Responsible People or Responsible Persons.

blocks.caption: The seven duties in section 45.25(2) of the ACNC Regulations 2022
head: Paragraph
Duty
What it means in practice
rows: Exercise powers and discharge duties with the care and diligence a reasonable individual would exercise as a Responsible Person of the charity
Prepare for meetings, read papers, ask questions, and understand the charity's activities and finances
Act in good faith in the charity's best interests and to further its purposes
Decisions serve the charitable purpose, not a sponsor, faction or personal agenda
Not misuse their position
No using the role to gain an advantage for themselves or others, or to harm the charity
Not misuse information obtained in performing their duties
Confidential board information stays confidential and is not used for personal gain
Disclose perceived or actual material conflicts of interest
Declare conflicts, including related party transactions, through the channel the regulation specifies
Ensure the charity's financial affairs are managed responsibly
Appropriate, tailored financial systems, such as expenditure approval procedures and suitable insurance
Not allow the charity to operate while insolvent
Monitor solvency and act before debts are incurred that the charity cannot pay

blocks.text: The regulation's notes add that Standard 5 sets out some of the more significant duties only; other Australian laws, including common law and equity, impose further duties, and some may require a higher standard. A charity that is also a company, incorporated association or trust should therefore read Standard 5 alongside its own governing law.

sections.heading: Why does the standard put the obligation on the charity rather than the board member?

blocks.text: Standard 5 is framed as an obligation on the charity because its object is public confidence. Section 45.25(1) says the standard aims to ensure Responsible Persons behave as if their relationship with the charity were fiduciary, and to give members, donors, employees, volunteers and beneficiaries confidence that the charity is acting to prevent non compliance and will identify and remedy it if it occurs.

That framing makes induction and training a compliance control rather than a courtesy. A charity cannot show it took reasonable steps to ensure compliance with duties its board was never told about. The ACNC says that because the standards are high level principles, each charity decides how to comply but must be able to show its steps are appropriate to its size, purposes and activities; a larger charity or one with vulnerable beneficiaries may need to do more.

sections.heading: What steps does the ACNC suggest so board members understand their duties?

blocks.text: The ACNC's [Governance Standards guidance](https://www.acnc.gov.au/for-charities/manage-your-charity/governance-hub/governance-standards) lists steps a charity can take to meet Standard 5. Several are directly about awareness and training.

items: Bring the duties to Responsible Persons' attention, for example by giving them a copy of the ACNC guidance, setting the duties out in a letter of appointment, or including them in a board or committee charter.
Regularly provide information or training to refresh their knowledge, such as advising them of relevant ACNC webinars.
Request that Responsible Persons undertake relevant training about their duties.
Encourage Responsible Persons to prepare for, attend and participate in meetings.
Have processes for the responsible management of money.
Have processes to manage conflicts of interest.
Take action if Responsible Persons are failing to meet their duties.

blocks.text: The ACNC also offers a self evaluation tool that asks charities to describe the practical steps they take and list the relevant policies or procedures, and a Governance Standards quiz. Recording completion of those tools by each board member is simple evidence of the "bring to attention" and "regular information" steps. Guidance on presenting this to the board itself is in [how to report training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board).

sections.heading: How must conflicts of interest be disclosed under Standard 5?

blocks.text: Section 45.25(3) sets the channel for disclosing a perceived or actual material conflict of interest, and board members should be trained on the channel that applies to their charity's structure. A director discloses to the other directors; a director of a corporate trustee discloses to the trustee's other directors; where neither applies and the charity is a company (which the Act defines broadly), disclosure goes to members; in any other case, unless the Commissioner provides otherwise, disclosure goes to the ACNC Commissioner in the approved form.

The regulation notes that a material conflict includes a related party transaction, and that a Responsible Person may disclose a conflict through a standing notice with ongoing effect. A conflicts register, updated at each meeting and signed off by each member, is the usual evidence. The ACNC's conflicts of interest and related party transactions tools support this process.

sections.heading: What protections apply to board members who act properly?

blocks.text: Subdivision 45-C provides four protections. If a Responsible Person meets one, section 45.100 treats the charity as having taken all reasonable steps to ensure compliance, and section 45.25(4) treats the person as having complied with the duties. Training should explain each, because they describe the behavior the standard rewards.

items: **Protection 1 (45.105):** relying in good faith, after an independent assessment, on information or advice from a reliable employee, a professional adviser or expert, another Responsible Person within their area, or an authorized committee.

**Protection 2 (45.110), the business judgment rule:** making a decision in good faith for a proper purpose, without a material personal interest, after informing oneself appropriately, and rationally believing it is in the charity's best interests. It relates to the care and diligence duty.
**Protection 3 (45.115):** for insolvent trading, having reasonable grounds to expect, and expecting, solvency when the debt was incurred, or taking all reasonable steps to prevent the debt.
**Protection 4 (45.120):** being unable to take part in management at the relevant time because of illness or another good reason.

blocks.text: Protection 1 depends on an "independent assessment" of the information, judged against the person's knowledge of the charity and the complexity of its operations. Board members who have not been trained to read financial statements will struggle to show that assessment, which is a practical argument for financial literacy content in board induction.

sections.heading: How do Standard 5 duties map to board training and evidence?

blocks.text: The ACNC does not require training records to be submitted, but a charity must be able to provide evidence of meeting the standards if asked. The table below is an original mapping of each duty to the board training and evidence that would demonstrate reasonable steps.

blocks.text: Acknowledgment records are discussed on the [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation) page, and a broader method for linking obligations to training is in [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

sections.heading: What happens if a charity does not comply, and who is exempt?

blocks.text: Compliance with the Governance Standards is a condition of ACNC registration, and failure to comply may lead to the Commissioner's enforcement powers, including warnings or directions, or to revocation of registration, which can cost the charity access to government funding, exemptions and concessions. The ACNC says it focuses on serious or deliberate breaches, giving examples such as diverting money to non charitable purposes, not disclosing serious conflicts of interest, or gross negligence with finances.

The Governance Standards do not apply to Basic Religious Charities, a limited category of charities with the purpose of advancing religion that meet further criteria. Charities operating overseas must also meet the External Conduct Standards. As at November 2026 the Regulations 2022 compilation in force dates from November 1, 2023. Standard 4, which sits alongside Standard 5, requires charities to check that Responsible Persons are not disqualified, so induction often covers both.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats each paragraph of section 45.25 as a defined obligation linked to a board learning outcome, an assessment point and an evidence record. That lets a charity show the ACNC, on request, which duty each induction or refresher item covers and which Responsible Person completed it.

faqs.q: Is board training mandatory for Australian charities?
faqs.a: Not in those words. Standard 5 requires the charity to take reasonable steps to ensure Responsible Persons are subject to and comply with the duties. The ACNC's suggested steps include regularly providing information or training and requesting that Responsible Persons undertake training, so most charities use training as the main way to show reasonable steps.

faqs.q: Who counts as a Responsible Person?
faqs.a: The ACNC uses the term for the people who govern a charity, such as board or committee members, directors and trustees. Where a charity is a trust with a corporate trustee, the directors of that trustee are covered, and section 45.25(3) sets a specific conflict disclosure channel for them.

faqs.q: Do charities have to send evidence of compliance to the ACNC?
faqs.a: No. The ACNC says a charity does not need to submit anything to show it meets the Governance Standards, but it must be able to provide evidence if requested. Keeping signed appointment letters, induction and training records, and a conflicts register is the practical way to be ready.

faqs.q: Does Governance Standard 5 apply to Basic Religious Charities?
faqs.a: No. The ACNC states that the Governance Standards do not apply to Basic Religious Charities. A Basic Religious Charity must, however, take reasonable steps to join the National Redress Scheme if required, or it loses that status and the standards then apply.

factCheck.claim: Section 45.25(2) of the ACNC Regulations 2022 requires a registered entity to take reasonable steps to ensure responsible entities are subject to and comply with seven listed duties
Section 45.25(1) object: fiduciary standard of behavior and public confidence that the entity prevents, identifies and remedies non compliance

Section 45.25(3) conflict disclosure channels (other directors, other directors of trustee, members, or Commissioner in approved form); notes on related party transactions and standing notices; note 3 on financial systems, expenditure approval and insurance
Sections 45.100 to 45.120: four protections including the business judgment rule (45.110) and insolvency protection (45.115); meeting a protection means all reasonable steps were taken
ACNC suggested steps for Standard 5 include letters of appointment or charter, regular information or training, requesting training, conflicts processes and taking action on failures

Governance Standards are a condition of registration; breaches may lead to warnings, directions or revocation; ACNC focuses on serious or deliberate breaches; standards do not apply to Basic Religious Charities; no submission needed but evidence on request
ACNC self-evaluation tool asks charities to describe practical steps and list relevant policies or procedures
